title: Agbeli Kaklo
localName: Agbeli kaklo — bankye krakro, cassava balls
author: Fafa Gilbert
desc: Grated cassava with the juice extracted, blended with onion and deep-fried at constant medium heat — the comfort food of the southern Volta.
longDesc: Agbeli kaklo is the cassava ball of the Volta Region, sold for as little as twenty Ghana pesewas and described as the comfort food from Volta. One large cassava is soaked overnight, grated, and the juice extracted, then the onion is blended into the drained cassava with salt and optional chilli and spring onion. It deep-fries at constant medium heat, avoiding overcrowding, until golden brown. It is known as agbeli kaklo in Ewe and bankye krakro in Ashanti — and a former president is recorded as having stopped his convoy at Anloga to buy it.
ingredients: Sunflower or coconut oil, for frying
equipment: Cloth or sack, for extracting the juice
steps: Extract the juice, pressing the grated cassava in a cloth.
Blend the onion into the drained cassava.
Season with salt, and add the chilli and spring onions if using.
Deep fry at constant medium heat, avoiding pan overcrowding.
Fry until golden brown, then drain and serve warm.
chefTips: Constant medium heat is her instruction and it is the key to this snack. High heat browns the outside while the cassava inside stays raw, and raw cassava is not just unpleasant but unsafe.
Extract the juice properly. Wet grated cassava will not hold a ball and will spit violently in oil.
Avoid overcrowding the pan — her own words. Crowded cassava balls steam and fall apart.
Soaking overnight is her step and it softens the tuber for grating. Another documented version drains the grated cassava under a stone instead.
Golden brown is the only cue any source gives. Nobody publishes a time or a temperature.
Blend the onion INTO the cassava rather than mixing it in. It distributes through the dough properly that way.
The names are regional: agbeli kaklo in Ewe, bankye krakro in Ashanti, for the same thing.
commonMistakes: Frying at high heat, leaving raw cassava inside.
Skipping the soak, which makes grating much harder.
Mixing the onion in rather than blending it.
sources: Quantities from a plantain-and-cassava post by Fafa Gilbert dated 4 March 2018. SINGLE-PASS and therefore unverified. Ingredients as printed: 1 large Cassava; 1 large Onion; Sunflower or Coconut oil for frying; 1 Green Chilli (Optional); 15g of chopped Spring Onions (optional); Salt to taste.
Her steps as printed: soak the peeled cassava overnight; grate; extract the juice; blend the onion into the drained cassava; 'Deep fry at constant medium heat, avoiding pan overcrowding'.
THE NAMES, quoted from her: 'Agbeli Kaklo or Bankye Krakro as known in the Ewe and Ashanti language respectively'.

THE CULTURAL SOURCE, and the better-provenanced one: Jemima Achivors, Graphic Online, Opinion section, 'Nov - 29 - 2019', 'Agbelikaklo: the comfort food from Volta'. NO QUANTITIES. Confirmed across two fetches: 'core ingredients of grated cassava, onions and salt which are mixed into smaller balls and fried in hot oil until it turns golden brown'; origin given as 'the southern part of the Volta Region'; price 'as low as 20 Ghana pesewas'; and a named vendor, Abra Degboe, in Ho. It also records that former President Rawlings stopped his convoy for it at Anloga.

A THIRD DOCUMENTED VERSION, with a different preparation: Pulse Ghana, byline the site's own name, printed 29 March 2018. SINGLE-PASS, NO QUANTITIES. Its method drains the grated cassava under a stone 'for some hours or overnight', sieves it to remove chaff, dries it 'in the sun for some few minutes', then fries 'until golden brown'.

THE DISAGREEMENT, unreconciled: Graphic describes simply grated cassava with onion and salt; Pulse drains under a stone, sieves and SUN-DRIES the dough; Fafa Gilbert soaks the cassava overnight and extracts the juice. Three different preparations of the same snack. NO SOURCE GIVES A DONENESS CUE BEYOND 'GOLDEN', and none gives a frying time or temperature.

A SAFETY POINT not stated by any source but following from the ingredient: raw cassava contains cyanogenic glycosides, so the constant-medium-heat instruction is doing safety work as well as texture work. That reasoning is labelled as editorial.
NO YIELD is printed by any source. The four servings above is an editorial reading of one large cassava.

FOR THE PLANTAIN VERSION of the same fritter family, see GHA048 (krakro) and GHA057 (kaaklo). The names overlap confusingly: kaklo attaches to both the cassava and the plantain fritter depending on the source.
storage: Same day. They go soft and heavy.
healthBenefits: Cassava is gluten-free and supplies resistant starch.
Draining the juice removes some of cassava's water-soluble cyanogenic compounds.
Cheap and filling, which is the point of the snack.
culturalNote: Agbeli kaklo at twenty pesewas a ball is street food at its most democratic, and the story of a head of state halting a motorcade at Anloga to buy some is the best endorsement any Ghanaian snack has on record. In Ashanti it is bankye krakro and nobody would mistake it for the plantain version.
